title: Convergence plot with fitted slopes: what is the observed order?
summary: The standard test that a numerical method converges at its design rate. Error is plotted against step size on log-log axes, so an error that scales as a power of h becomes a straight line whose slope is the observed order.

media.alt: Log-log plot of error against step size h: three lines for methods of order 1, 2 and 4, with a dotted round-off floor near 1e-14.
media.caption: Reference render of class F5.1 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: What is the observed order?
read_the_figure.axes: x: step size h, logarithmic, from 1e-3 to about 0.3. y: error (in one chosen norm), logarithmic, from about 1e-14 to 1.
look_at: Is each series a straight line? Count how many decades of h it stays straight over.
What is the slope of each line, read from numbers and not from the angle?
Does any line bend or flatten at small h? Where, and how close to the floor line?
Are the lines roughly parallel to the reference slope you expected (1, 2, 4)?
as_drawn: Three series with nominal orders 1, 2 and 4 are drawn: error = 0.8 h^p, from h = 1e-3 to h about 0.32.
The dotted floor is at 1e-14. The order-4 series ends at about 8e-13, still about 80 times above it.
The legend gives the nominal order only. The fitted slope is not printed on the figure, which the class requires: a trustworthy version prints it beside each line.
The x axis spans 2.5 decades and the y axis 14, so a slope-1 line looks gentle. Read slopes from numbers, not from angles.
read_the_figure.proves: Straight lines of the expected slope over a clear range of h are evidence that the method and its implementation reach the design order. They do not prove the answer is correct: a wrong but consistent equation also converges.
if_wrong: Slope smaller than the design order: a bug, a low-order boundary treatment, a non-smooth solution, or a reference solution that is itself too coarse.
Line flattens at small h: you have reached the round-off floor or the tolerance of an inner solver. Do not fit a slope there.
Line wiggles or curves at large h: not yet in the asymptotic range, so the error model does not apply yet.
must_check: log-log axes: a power law e = C h^p only becomes a straight line when both axes are logarithmic.
slope fitted and printed: the order is a number, so print it; the eye cannot tell a slope of 1.8 from 2.
floor line: it marks where round-off takes over, so the reader knows which part of the data is meaningful.

terms.meaning: The spacing between grid points or time levels. Halving it doubles the work for a one-dimensional problem.
The difference between the computed and the exact answer at a fixed final time, measured in a stated norm.
The exponent p in e = C h^p. A method of order p cuts the error by 2^p when h is halved.
The range of small h in which the leading error term dominates, so the log-log line is straight.
The smallest error a floating-point computation can reach, set by machine epsilon (about 2.2e-16 in double precision), not by the method.
Both axes logarithmic: equal distances are equal ratios, and a power law is a straight line.

remember: e = C h^p gives ln e = ln C + p ln h: a line of slope p.
Observed order p = ln(e1/e2) / ln(h1/h2) from two runs.
Halving h: order 1 gives half the error, order 2 a quarter, order 4 one sixteenth.
Fit the slope only on the straight part, away from the floor.
The floor is set by round-off, so refining h further cannot help.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Each marker is one run at one step size. Lines join the runs of one method; colour and marker shape separate methods so the plot survives greyscale. Position on x is the step size, position on y is the error, both on log scales. The dotted horizontal line is a reference, not data.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language first: if the error is a constant times h to some power, then taking logarithms turns the power into a multiplier, and a multiplier is a slope. So the steepness of the line is the order. A steeper line means the error shrinks faster each time you refine. On a linear plot the three methods would all hug the axes and none of the slopes could be compared.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: A slope read by eye is unreliable when the axes have different decade lengths. A fit over a range that includes the floor or the pre-asymptotic region gives the wrong order. Using a different norm, or a final time that changes with h, changes the apparent order. And convergence is not correctness: the lines only show that the method approaches its own limit.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A table of observed orders p_k between successive refinements shows the same thing numerically and exposes drift. Plotting error against cost (a work-precision diagram, class F5.9) compares methods fairly, because a higher order method may cost more per step. A local-slope plot shows where the asymptotic range starts.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Print the fitted slope beside each line, shade the fitting window, draw a small reference triangle of slope 1, 2 and 4, and set the axes so one decade in x has the same length as one decade in y.

steps.title: The error model and the line
steps.note: A straight line in ln h with slope p. Replace ln by log10 and nothing changes.

steps.title: Observed order from two runs
steps.note: For a refinement ratio of 2 this is log base 2 of e1/e2. Compute it between each pair of neighbouring runs.

steps.title: Where round-off takes over
steps.note: Truncation falls with h while round-off grows like 1/h, so there is a best step. For a forward difference (p = 1, C of order 1) this gives about 1e-8, the number on the atlas page.

worked.title: Reading the order from the reference render
worked.problem: Using the figure: (1) What are the three observed orders? (2) For the order-4 method, by what factor does the error fall when h is halved, and does the figure agree? (3) At what h would the order-4 line reach the 1e-14 floor, and is that inside the plotted range?

solution.text: (1) Take the order-2 line: it runs from about 8e-7 at h = 1e-3 to about 8e-2 at h = 0.32. That is five decades of error over 2.5 decades of h.

The other two lines give 1 and 4 in the same way: about 2.5 decades of error for the top line over 2.5 decades of h would be slope 1, and about 10 decades over the same 2.5 decades of h (slope 4) for the steep one.
(2) Halving h multiplies the error by 2 to the minus p.
The figure agrees: neighbouring order-4 markers, a factor of 1.7 apart in h, differ in error by about 1.7^4, roughly a factor of 8.

worked.answer: Orders 1, 2 and 4. The order-4 line meets the floor at h of about 3.3e-4, which is below the smallest plotted h of 1e-3, so the plotted range is entirely above the floor and fitting a slope on all of it is legitimate.

analyze.q: The three lines meet at the right-hand end (h about 0.3). What does that say about the constants C of the three methods?
analyze.hint: At one h the errors are equal, so C h^p is equal for different p.

analyze.q: A colleague fits a straight line through all the points including the flat part near the floor and reports order 3.2. What went wrong, and how do you redo it?
analyze.hint: Which part of the data does the error model describe?

analyze.q: Why is it useful that the slope is independent of C?
analyze.hint: Two implementations of the same method can have different C.

evaluate.q: Is a clean slope of 2 enough to say a code solves the intended equation correctly?
evaluate.hint: Think of a method of order 2 applied to the wrong right-hand side.

create: Redraw the figure with the fitted slope printed beside each line and a shaded fitting window.
Add a fourth series that flattens at the floor and mark in a different style the points you excluded from the fit.

checks.hint: Take the logarithm of e = C h^p.
checks.answer: Because the error is a power of h; the logarithm turns it into ln e = ln C + p ln h, a straight line whose slope is p.

checks.q: A method gives error 3.2e-3 at h = 0.1 and 2.0e-4 at h = 0.05. What is the observed order?
checks.hint: Use the formula with a refinement ratio of 2.

checks.q: A line is straight at large h and then goes flat at small h. Name the cause and say what you should not do.
checks.hint: What does the floor line mark?
checks.answer: The error has hit the round-off floor (or a solver tolerance); refining further gives no gain. Do not include the flat part when fitting the slope, and consider a smaller-error norm or higher precision if you must go lower.
